passage: I'm Wasim, and last term maths felt like sand slipping through my fingers. Numbers wouldn't stay put. If Ammi said "Be back by quarter to six," I didn't know what that looked like on the clock. In class, when Arnab Sir said "Quick, how many minutes till lunch?", my chest went tight and my mind went white. But I could draw anything. My notebook margins were full of horses. Then Arnab Sir stopped asking me quick questions in front of everyone. He gave me a cardboard clock with hands I could move, and we counted in fives with bottle caps, again and again, no scolding. Now I can find quarter to six. I drew a horse on that cardboard clock, right at the six.

qa.q: What did Arnab Sir give Wasim to practise with?
qa.a: A cardboard clock with hands Wasim could move.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel when asked a quick maths question in class, and what shows it?
qa.a: Panic; Wasim's chest went tight and Wasim's mind went white.

qa.q: Which change by Arnab Sir made progress possible?
qa.a: He stopped the quick public questions and used hands-on things like the clock and bottle caps, repeating patiently without scolding.

qa.q: How might Arnab Sir see Wasim's horse drawing on the clock?
qa.a: He may see it as a sign that Wasim now feels safe and even proud around the clock that once caused panic.

grounding: It shows a child who struggles with time and numbers and panics in maths though good at art, helped by hands-on materials, repetition and no shaming.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 4B, class shop week Rafiq priced the pencils beautifully; his labels had drawings of each item. But when Mehak bought an eraser for seven rupees with a ten-rupee coin, Rafiq froze. He counted the coins in the box three times, went red and whispered, "I can't do it." He left the counter and hid in the reading corner. In writing time the same afternoon he wrote a funny story about a shopkeeper parrot, full of lively words. What I did next: I gave Rafiq a tray of real coins and a number line, and we practised change privately, one small amount a day. No one is timed at the shop now. By Friday he gave three rupees change, checked it twice, and grinned. - Madhuri, class teacher

qa.q: How much did the eraser cost in the class shop?
qa.a: Seven rupees.

qa.q: What does Rafiq hiding in the reading corner suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he felt panic and embarrassment when he couldn't work out the change in front of others.

qa.q: What small steps did Madhuri take that helped Rafiq?
qa.a: Madhuri gave him real coins and a number line, practised privately one small amount a day, and stopped timing children at the shop.

qa.q: How might Mehak have been affected if Madhuri had scolded Rafiq at the counter?
qa.a: Mehak and the other children might have learned to see Rafiq as slow, and his shame would have grown.

grounding: A teacher sees a child who panics over money though he is strong in writing, and uses hands-on coins and patient repetition without shaming.

passage: Sunday night Imran's report card is on the table and I keep looking at it. Maths and reading marked "needs support" again. At lunch Bhabhi said, loud enough for him to hear, "Our Pihu reads English novels already." Imran went quiet and pushed his rice around. Part of me wanted to book the strict tuition teacher the whole colony talks about. Part of me wanted to hide him from everyone. Instead I rang his class teacher and asked for a meeting. She said the school can help with extra reading time. Then I pinned his clay elephant on the fridge photo wall and told him it's the best one in the building. He slept with the report card under his pillow. I don't know why. I'll ask tomorrow. - Charu (his very tired mother)

qa.q: Where did Charu put a picture of Imran's clay elephant?
qa.a: On the fridge photo wall.

qa.q: What was Charu worried about after the report card, and why did it feel like a pull in two directions?
qa.a: Charu was torn between pushing Imran with strict tuition and protecting him from everyone's comments.

qa.q: Which choice helped keep the family steady?
qa.a: Charu rang the class teacher to plan help with the school, and also celebrated Imran's clay elephant.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when Bhabhi talked about Pihu?
qa.a: He probably felt compared and small; he went quiet and pushed his rice around.

grounding: It shows a parent who worries about grades and relatives' comments, feels torn between pushing and protecting, and works with the school while praising her child's other talents.

passage: In the milk queue outside the dairy, Patil-kaka asked Darshan loudly, "So your Zubin still can't read the bus board?" A few people laughed. Darshan's face went hot. All the way home he argued with himself. Send the boy to the tuition master in the next town, three hours a day? Or keep him home, away from these remarks? That evening he sat with Zubin, who was sanding a little wooden bullock cart for his cousin. The wheels actually turned. "You made this without a drawing?" Darshan asked. "I saw it in my head, Papa." Next morning Darshan went to the school, not the tuition master. The teacher agreed to sit with them both every Saturday. At the village fair, the wooden cart won a ribbon, and Darshan stood right beside it.

qa.q: What was Zubin sanding in the evening?
qa.a: A little wooden bullock cart for his cousin.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after the comment in the milk queue, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and torn; his face went hot and he argued with himself all the way home.

qa.q: What turning point settled Darshan's choice?
qa.a: Seeing Zubin build the cart from his head made him go to the school to work with the teacher instead of the long tuition.

qa.q: How does Zubin likely feel when his father stands beside the cart at the fair?
qa.a: He probably feels proud and backed by his father, seeing his talent valued in front of the village.

grounding: It shows a father worried by others' comments, torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and celebrates his son's other talent.

passage: Fatima could tell the whole story of the Viking raid on Lindisfarne as if she had been in the boat: the cold spray, the bells, the monks running. In class discussions in her Oslo school, everyone listened. But in timed tests her answers came out short and misspelled, and she always ran out of time halfway. Her history mark said average. Her head said she knew everything. Lars, the learning support teacher, noticed the gap. "Would you do an assessment with the school psychologist? It would show how you learn best." The report came back weeks later. Fatima got extra time and could type her answers. In the next test she wrote four full pages. When the mark came back, she read the comment twice: "This is what you really know."

qa.q: What could Fatima type after the assessment?
qa.a: Her answers, and she also got extra time.

qa.q: What does it suggest that Fatima's head 'said she knew everything'?
qa.a: It suggests she felt frustrated, because she knew the history well but the timed, written tests didn't show it.

qa.q: What was the key step that changed Fatima's results?
qa.a: Lars suggested an assessment, which led to extra time and typing, so her knowledge could show.

qa.q: How might Lars see Fatima's four pages compared with her old tests?
qa.a: Lars would see that her real ability was there all along and only the test conditions hid it.

grounding: It shows a teenager who tells stories brilliantly but struggles with spelling and reading speed under time limits, and how an assessment and accommodations show what she truly knows.

passage: The exam room for students with extra time was a small classroom on the second floor, with a fan that clicked. "You okay?" Pranav asked at the door. He'd come up just to walk Eshaan in. "Honestly? My hands are shaking. Last year I only finished half the paper." "Last year you didn't have the extra time or the reader." The reader was a young woman from the school office who would read the questions aloud. Eshaan sat down. When she read question four, about a village during a flood, he closed his eyes and saw it: the brown water, the roofs, a goat on a door. He wrote it out in rough spelling, but full. Afterwards Pranav waited on the steps. "Well?" "I finished," Eshaan said. "For the first time, I finished."

qa.q: What did the reader from the school office do?
qa.a: She read the questions aloud to Eshaan.

qa.q: Why were Eshaan's hands shaking before the exam?
qa.a: He was anxious because last year he only finished half the paper.

qa.q: What difference did the permitted support make?
qa.a: With extra time and a reader, Eshaan could picture and write full answers and finished the paper for the first time.

qa.q: How does Pranav show he sees Eshaan's struggle?
qa.a: Pranav walks him in, reminds him that the conditions are different now, and waits afterwards to hear how it went.

grounding: It shows a teenager who thinks in pictures but struggles with reading speed, whose permitted accommodations let him show what he knows.

subtype: Teacher noticing a gap between effort and results [Observer]
passage: "Swati, stay back a minute?" "Did I do something wrong, Ma'am?" "No. The opposite. In class you explained why the river changes course better than anyone. Where did that come from?" "I just... see it. The water pushing on the soft bank." "But your written test has three lines." "I know." Swati looks at the floor. "I try. I write it again and again. It comes out wrong." "I believe you try. I've watched you." Urmila, the geography teacher, pulls a chair over. "Can I ask your parents to meet the counsellor about a screening? It checks how your brain handles reading and writing." "So I'm not lazy?" "Lazy people don't rewrite things again and again. And I won't ask you to read aloud without warning anymore. Deal?" "Deal."

qa.q: Which topic did Swati explain better than anyone in class?
qa.a: Why the river changes course.

qa.q: Why does Swati ask, 'So I'm not lazy?'
qa.a: Swati seems worried that the short written work looks lazy, and hopes the teacher sees the effort.

qa.q: What choice does Urmila make instead of blaming Swati?
qa.a: Urmila suggests a screening through the counsellor and stops asking Swati to read aloud without warning.

qa.q: How might Swati's self-image change after this talk?
qa.a: Swati may stop feeling lazy and start seeing that the ideas are strong while writing is hard.

grounding: A teacher notices strong oral answers but weak written work, suggests screening, avoids reading aloud on the spot and values the student's ideas.

subtype: Teacher noticing a gap between effort and results [Observer]
passage: My name is Gopika, and I've taught maths for eleven years. I still think about Parveen, from two batches ago. She was the most careful student I had. Neat margins, every step written. And yet her answers were wrong in strange ways: 36 became 63, a plus sign read as a minus. At first I wrote "careless" in red. I'm not proud of that. Then I sat beside her during a test and watched. She was not careless. She was checking every line, lips moving, and still the digits slid. I stopped using red for those slips. I asked her family about a screening, and I started marking her method separately from her final number. Her method marks were among the best in the class. She stood a little straighter after that.

qa.q: What did Gopika write in red at first?
qa.a: Careless.

qa.q: What does Gopika saying 'I'm not proud of that' show about how Gopika feels now?
qa.a: It shows regret; looking back, Gopika feels she misjudged Parveen's effort.

qa.q: What did Gopika change after watching Parveen during a test?
qa.a: Gopika stopped marking the slips in red, asked the family about a screening and marked Parveen's method separately.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when her method marks were among the best?
qa.a: She probably felt seen and proud, since her careful effort finally counted; she stood a little straighter.

grounding: A teacher sees careful effort with number errors, suggests screening and values the student's thinking, separating learning difference from lack of effort.

passage: 14 March Did it. Finally went to Jaya ma'am's office hours and said the words: "I have dyslexia. Could I get the reading list early, and extra time in the mid-sems?" My voice was shaking and I stared at her plant the whole time. I'd practised it for a week. She just nodded and said, "Of course. Thank you for telling me. Would audio versions help?" That's it. No face. No sigh. All this semester I've been listening to the chapters on my phone at double speed on the bus and dictating notes with the voice tool. I thought using them was cheating. It isn't. It's how I read. Got back my essay today too: "Sharp argument." Pinned it above the desk. - Santosh

qa.q: What did Santosh ask Jaya ma'am for?
qa.a: The reading list early and extra time in the mid-sems.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel while asking, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Santosh felt embarrassed and nervous; the voice was shaking and Santosh stared at the plant, after practising for a week.

qa.q: Which choice turned out to be worth the risk?
qa.a: Santosh told the tutor about the dyslexia and asked for support, and was met with understanding and an offer of audio versions.

qa.q: How does Jaya ma'am seem to see Santosh's request?
qa.a: She treats it as normal and reasonable, even thanking Santosh for telling her.

grounding: It shows a young adult who uses audio and voice tools, feels embarrassed to ask for extra time, and is met with understanding when sharing the difference.

passage: Dolma: ok so I'm telling my manager tomorrow Rukmini: about the dyslexia? Dolma: yes. I keep messing up the handover sheets when I rush Rukmini: what are you going to say Dolma: that I'm good at the work, I just need the checklist in a bigger font and a few extra minutes for reports Rukmini: that's clear and fair Dolma: what if he thinks I lied in the interview Rukmini: you didn't lie. you got the job because you're good [Next evening] Dolma: he said "why didn't you say earlier, we'll fix the template" Dolma: he also said my customer calls are the best on the team Rukmini: TOLD YOU Dolma: I actually feel proud? not embarrassed. weird Rukmini: not weird. earned

qa.q: What two changes did Dolma plan to ask for?
qa.a: The checklist in a bigger font and a few extra minutes for reports.

qa.q: What was Dolma worried about before talking to the manager?
qa.a: Dolma was worried the manager would think Dolma had lied in the interview.

qa.q: What small step helped Dolma prepare for the talk?
qa.a: Dolma practised the exact words with Rukmini, keeping them short and clear about strengths and needs.

qa.q: How does the manager's reaction show how he sees Dolma?
qa.a: He sees a capable worker; he offers to fix the template and praises Dolma's customer calls.

grounding: It shows a young adult who feels nervous about sharing dyslexia at work, asks for simple adjustments and finds understanding and pride.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday Jagdish, two, screamed and dropped to the floor when the hand dryer roared in the washroom. He covered his ears and would not go back in. At sand play he pulled his hands out as if the sand burned. What I did: we now use paper towels with him, and the dryer stays off when he is inside. I put dry rice in a small tub; he watched, then poked one finger in. We will not force the sand. - Swati, caregiver

qa.q: What does the daycare now use with Jagdish instead of the dryer?
qa.a: Paper towels.

qa.q: How can you tell the hand dryer upset Jagdish?
qa.a: He was frightened and overwhelmed by the noise: he screamed, dropped to the floor, covered his ears and would not go back in.

qa.q: Which choice by Swati was gentle rather than forceful?
qa.a: Swati offered a small tub of dry rice and let him poke one finger in, without forcing the sand.

qa.q: How might the other children's day change because of these small adjustments?
qa.a: The room would likely stay calmer, since Jagdish is not screaming in the washroom and can join play his own way.

grounding: A caregiver's note on a toddler who screams at hand dryers and refuses a texture, using a calm setup and gentle exposure instead of force.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Harsha spins and spins until she tumbles into the hay, laughing. Then she climbs up and crashes into the hay again. At dinner she bumps her head against her mother Reena's arm, hard, over and over. The neighbours say, "Stop her, she'll get wild." Reena does not scold. She ties a sack swing to the neem tree. Harsha swings, stomach down, for a long time. Afterwards she sits quietly in Reena's lap and eats her roti.

qa.q: What does Reena tie to the neem tree?
qa.a: A sack swing.

qa.q: What does Harsha sitting quietly in Reena's lap after swinging suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels calmer and settled once her body has had enough movement.

qa.q: Which choice by Reena worked better than scolding?
qa.a: She gave Harsha a safe swing for the spinning and crashing her body wanted, instead of stopping her.

qa.q: How do the neighbours see Harsha's spinning differently from Reena?
qa.a: The neighbours see it as wildness to stop, while Reena seems to see a need her daughter's body has.

grounding: It shows a toddler who seeks spinning and crashing, and a mother who offers a calmer, safe outlet instead of force.

passage: I'm Arohi. In Class 5, school felt like being scratched all day. The label in my uniform collar poked like a thorn. The tube lights buzzed. The bell rang right above our door, so loud my teeth hurt. By lunch I was snapping at everyone, and then I'd go silent. Francis Sir noticed me holding my ears at the bell. He didn't say I was rude. He asked, "What bothers you most here?" I told him everything. Mummy cut out the labels that night. Francis Sir moved my seat to the window, away from the bell and the buzzing light, and let me wear soft ear covers at bell time. The next week I didn't snap once. I even laughed at recess.

qa.q: Where did Francis Sir move Arohi's seat?
qa.a: To the window, away from the bell and the buzzing light.

qa.q: Why was Arohi snapping at everyone by lunch?
qa.a: The poking label, buzzing lights and loud bell made Arohi feel scratched and worn out all day.

qa.q: What small changes helped Arohi most?
qa.a: Cutting out the labels, a window seat away from the bell and light, and ear covers at bell time.

qa.q: How might Francis Sir's question have felt different to Arohi than a scolding?
qa.a: It showed Arohi that the discomfort was believed, so Arohi could explain instead of feeling blamed for being rude.

grounding: It shows a child who cannot bear labels, lights and the school bell and seems irritable, helped by small changes like a quiet seat and ear covers.

passage: Class 3 teacher's note on Tenzin For two weeks Tenzin has been pale and grumpy after lunch. He sits with his arms folded, head down, and refuses to answer. Some children call him moody. Today I watched closely. In the canteen he covered his nose with his sleeve and ate almost nothing. Under the bright lights in the art room he squinted and put his head on his arms. What I did next: I let Tenzin eat his tiffin in the library corner with one friend, and I turned off the two lights above his table in art. I told his family what I saw. This afternoon he finished his tiffin and painted a mountain with three yaks. - Akash Sir

qa.q: Where does Tenzin now eat his tiffin?
qa.a: In the library corner with one friend.

qa.q: What does Tenzin covering his nose in the canteen suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the canteen smell bothered him a lot and made him unable to eat.

qa.q: Which of Akash Sir's steps was most useful, and why?
qa.a: Watching closely before judging; it showed the smell and lights were the problem, so small changes could fix them.

qa.q: How might the children who call Tenzin moody see him if they understood?
qa.a: They might see that he was uncomfortable, not moody, and be kinder when he goes quiet.

grounding: A teacher sees a child who seems withdrawn because of the canteen smell and bright lights, and small changes like a quieter place help a lot.

subtype: Family member misreading it as fussiness [Receiver]
passage: Monday. "Uma, it's only socks!" Gurpreet Bua snapped at the door. Uma pulled them off for the third time, crying that the seam bit her toes. "So dramatic," Bua muttered. They missed the school van. Wednesday. This time Bua knelt down. "Tell me what it feels like." Uma thought. "Like a line of ants that won't stop walking." Bua was quiet, then turned the socks inside out so the seam faced away. Uma wiggled her toes. "Better." The next Monday. Bua had bought two pairs of smooth socks without a ridge at the toe. Uma put them on by herself, first try. They reached the van early, and Bua let her pick the song on the walk.

qa.q: How did Bua turn the socks on Wednesday?
qa.a: Inside out, so the seam faced away.

qa.q: How did Uma feel on Monday when Bua called her dramatic?
qa.a: She felt upset and not believed; she was crying that the seam bit her toes.

qa.q: What turning point ended the sock battles?
qa.a: On Wednesday Bua knelt and asked what it felt like, listened, and tried a small change.

qa.q: How did Bua's view of Uma change across the week?
qa.a: Bua first saw her as dramatic, then believed her description and started solving the problem with her.

grounding: It shows a relative who first calls a child dramatic about clothes, then listens, believes her and tries small adjustments that end the daily battles.

subtype: Family member misreading it as fussiness [Receiver]
passage: "Abhinav, sit. You say your little one is fussy with food? Let me tell you about my Tashi. When he was nine, he would not eat dal if there was one lump in it. Rice touching the vegetables? He'd push the plate away and cry. I thought, this boy is spoilt. My mother-in-law said the same. Every dinner was a war. One night he whispered, 'Ama-la, the lumps feel like stones in my mouth. It makes me want to be sick.' Stones, Abhinav. He wasn't being clever. He was telling me. So I strained his dal smooth and gave him a plate with little walls. Just that. The wars stopped. Before you call her fussy, ask her what the food feels like. Then believe her." Dolma poured him more tea.

qa.q: What did Tashi say the lumps felt like?
qa.a: Like stones in his mouth.

qa.q: What did Dolma realise when Tashi whispered about the lumps?
qa.a: She realised he wasn't being clever or spoilt; he was honestly telling her how the food felt.

qa.q: What did Dolma change after Tashi's whisper, and why did it work?
qa.a: Dolma strained his dal smooth and gave him a plate with little walls; it worked because it answered what Tashi said the food felt like, and the wars stopped.

qa.q: What was dinner like for Tashi before Dolma listened?
qa.a: It was a daily war where he felt upset and was called spoilt, with food that felt like stones.

grounding: An elder recalls thinking her son was picky about food, then listening, believing him and making small adjustments that ended the daily battles.

passage: "So people think I'm restless. And fine, I am, a bit. My name's Vidya, I'm sixteen, and there's always a pen cap in my mouth. I tap my foot through every class. To study I need loud music, really loud, or my brain won't sit still. My best friend Nilesh is the opposite. At the school fest he wore ear defenders and ate only the plain parathas he brought from home. Some people laughed. But he knows himself. That's what we worked out together. We both have bodies that react strongly, just in different directions. So I carry a chewy bracelet instead of wrecking pens, and I ask to sit at the back so my tapping doesn't bother anyone. Nilesh plans his quiet corner before every event. It's not weird. It's a plan."

qa.q: What did Nilesh bring from home to the school fest?
qa.a: Plain parathas, and he wore ear defenders.

qa.q: How does Vidya seem to feel about being called restless?
qa.a: Vidya accepts it without shame and seems proud that Vidya and Nilesh understand themselves well enough to plan.

qa.q: What choices does Vidya make to manage the need for movement?
qa.a: Vidya carries a chewy bracelet instead of chewing pens and sits at the back so the tapping doesn't bother anyone.

qa.q: How might the people who laughed at Nilesh see him if they heard Vidya?
qa.a: They might see him as someone who knows what his body needs and plans for it, not as someone strange.

grounding: It shows a teenager who chews, fidgets and craves loud music and a friend who covers his ears and avoids foods, both using self-knowledge to plan.

passage: My brother Omkar is fifteen, and at our cousin's wedding I watched him closely. I can't say what was in his head, only what I saw. When the band started, he pressed both hands over his ears and stepped behind a pillar. At dinner he took only curd rice and left the fried items untouched. But he wasn't sulking. Before we went, he had asked Mummy which hall had the quiet garden, and he'd packed earplugs in his pocket. When the dancing began, he nodded to me and went out to that garden. Later he came back in for the photos, smiling properly. "I just needed ten minutes," he told me. "I know how much noise I can take." I'm Neelam, by the way. I used to call him boring. I don't now.

qa.q: What did Omkar take at dinner?
qa.a: Only curd rice.

qa.q: What does Omkar's line 'I know how much noise I can take' suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he understands his own needs and feels confident planning around them.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's choices helped him enjoy the wedding?
qa.a: He asked about the quiet garden in advance, carried earplugs and took a short break before the photos.

qa.q: How has Neelam's view of Omkar changed?
qa.a: Neelam used to call him boring, but now sees that he is managing the noise wisely.

grounding: A sibling watches a teenager who covers his ears in a crowd and avoids certain foods, and sees how his self-knowledge lets him plan.

passage: Maria: hey roomie! moving in tomorrow, anything I should know? Ganga: hi! yes, quick things so it's not awkward later Ganga: bright white light really gets to me, so I use a small lamp at night Ganga: and strong scents give me headaches, so no room spray if that's ok? Maria: totally fine. I have a lamp too Ganga: also I take the desk by the window, it helps me focus. you can pick the bed side Maria: deal. anything else? Ganga: that's it. I promise I'm not fussy, I just know what makes my week go better Maria: honestly this is helpful. I hate guessing [Two weeks later] Maria: saw you sat near the exit at the orientation talk Ganga: yes, crowds are easier from there Maria: smart. saving you the same seat for the next one

qa.q: Where does Ganga choose to sit at the orientation talk?
qa.a: Near the exit.

qa.q: Why does Ganga explain these needs before moving in?
qa.a: Ganga wants to avoid awkwardness later and seems worried about being seen as fussy.

qa.q: Which approach made the new roommate setup work?
qa.a: Ganga explained the needs briefly and early, and chose the desk and seat that ease the triggers.

qa.q: How does Maria see Ganga's explanation?
qa.a: Maria finds it helpful because Maria hates guessing, and offers to save Ganga's seat.

grounding: It shows a young adult who knows the triggers, chooses seating and routines to ease them and briefly explains these needs as self-care, not fussiness.

passage: The trainee teachers' bus from the block office always filled up by eight, so Gargi came at a quarter to and took the back window seat, where the breeze was steady and no one pressed against her. She wore her soft cotton kurta, never the stiff polyester uniform sari the others preferred. At the school, Irfan, another trainee, found her by the water tank during the loud morning assembly. "Skipping assembly?" "Only the loudspeaker part. It makes my head ring for hours. I told the headmistress; I'm back for the lesson." "She didn't mind?" "She said, 'Fine, as long as your class is ready.' And it always is." Irfan thought about it. "I get headaches from the loudspeaker too. I never thought I could say so." Gargi smiled. "You can. It's not fussiness. It's how I stay good at this."

qa.q: Which seat does Gargi take on the trainee teachers' bus?
qa.a: The back window seat, where the breeze was steady.

qa.q: What does Irfan realise during the talk?
qa.a: Irfan realises the loudspeaker gives Irfan headaches too, and that it is fine to say so, which Irfan had never thought possible.

qa.q: Which choices help Gargi stay well at work?
qa.a: Coming early for the window seat, wearing a soft cotton kurta and briefly explaining to the headmistress why she steps out of assembly.

qa.q: How might the headmistress see Gargi's request?
qa.a: She sees it as reasonable, since Gargi's class is always ready.

grounding: It shows a young adult who chooses seating, clothing and routines to ease her triggers and briefly explains her needs as self-care.
